en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Bhūtagāmavagga 12.
The Training Rule on Speaking Otherwise.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.

Now at that time, the Venerable Channa, having practiced improper conduct, while being questioned by the Saṅgha in the midst of the community regarding an offense, evaded the matter with irrelevant talk:
"Who has committed it? What has he committed? In what has he committed it? How has he committed it? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How can the Venerable Channa, when being questioned about an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, evade the matter with something else, saying:
‘Who has committed it? What has been committed? In what has one committed it? How has one committed it? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, Channa, that when being questioned about an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, you evade the matter with something else?”
“Who has fallen into [offense]? What has he fallen into? In what has he fallen? How has he fallen? Whom do you speak of? What do you say?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How is it, foolish man, that when you are being examined regarding an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, you evade one matter with another, saying:
'Who has fallen? What has he fallen into? In what has he fallen? How has he fallen? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?'?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth]."
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha lay the charge of evasive speech against the bhikkhu Channa.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be planted as follows:
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.”
This monk Channa, when being examined regarding an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, evades the matter with irrelevant talk.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha charge monk Channa with speaking evasively.
This is the motion.
Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa, when being examined regarding an offense in the midst of the Sangha, evades the matter by speaking otherwise than the truth.
The Sangha is pronouncing the charge of "speaking otherwise" against the bhikkhu Channa.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal charge against the monk Channa for speaking otherwise, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
The formal charge against the monk Channa for speaking otherwise has been brought by the Saṅgha.
“The Saṅgha approves; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Channa in many ways for his difficult-to-support nature … [as before] … and furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“‘For one who speaks evasively, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa, while being questioned regarding an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, evaded the matter by speaking of something else.”
Thinking, “I will commit an offense,” he remains silent and harasses the Saṅgha.
Those monks who are of few desires … [as before] … they criticize, grumble, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the Venerable Channa, when being questioned regarding an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, remain silent and harass the Saṅgha? … [as before] …
“Is it true, Channa, that while you were being questioned by the Saṅgha in the midst of the community regarding an offense, you remained silent and harassed the Saṅgha?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him … [as before] …
"How indeed, foolish man, can you, when being questioned by the Saṅgha in the midst of the community regarding an offense, remain silent and harass the Saṅgha?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him... [and so forth]."
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha lay the charge of harassment against the bhikkhu Channa.
And this, bhikkhus, is how it should be laid.”
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk Channa, while being questioned by the Saṅgha in the midst of the assembly regarding an offense, remains silent and harasses the Saṅgha.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha charge the bhikkhu Channa with being a harasser.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa, being questioned by the Saṅgha in the midst of the community regarding an offense, harasses the Saṅgha by remaining silent.
The Saṅgha charges the bhikkhu Channa with harassment.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the charging of the bhikkhu Channa with harassment, let him remain silent.
"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has imposed the *ropita* (formal act) of harassment upon the monk Channa.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it to be so."
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Channa in many ways for being difficult to support … [as before] … and furthermore,
monks, you should recite this training rule: “In the case of one who speaks otherwise or who harasses,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).”

One who speaks evasively is one who, when being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding a matter or an offense, not wishing to speak about it and not wishing to disclose it, prevaricates with something else, saying:
"Who has committed [an offense]? What has been committed? In what has one committed? How has one committed? Whom..."
"Speak! What do you say? This is called one who speaks evasively.

One who is "troublesome" is one who, when being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding a matter or an offense, does not wish to speak about it nor wishes to reveal it, and by remaining silent, causes trouble for the Saṅgha. This is called one who is troublesome.

When one has been charged with speaking evasively and, while being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding the matter or the offense, does not wish to speak about it nor wishes to reveal it, but evades the point by talking about something else, saying:

"Who has committed [an offense]? What has he committed? Regarding what has he committed? How has he committed it? Whom are you addressing? What are you saying?"—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

When one has been charged with causing trouble and, while being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding the matter or the offense, does not wish to speak about it nor wishes to reveal it, but remains silent and causes trouble for the Saṅgha—there is an offense of wrong-doing.

When one who has been charged with speaking otherwise is being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding either the matter or the offense, and not wishing to speak about it nor wishing to reveal it, evades the point by talking about something else, saying:

"Who has committed [an offense]? What has he committed? Regarding what has he committed? How has he committed it? Whom are you addressing? What are you saying?"—there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

When one who has been charged with causing trouble is being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha regarding either the matter or the offense, and not wishing to speak about it nor wishing to reveal it, remains silent and thereby causes trouble for the Saṅgha—there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is a legitimate legal procedure (*dhammakamma*) and one perceives it as such, yet one speaks otherwise and causes vexation, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If it is a legitimate legal procedure but one is uncertain of it, yet one speaks otherwise and causes vexation, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is a legitimate legal procedure but one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*), yet one speaks otherwise and causes vexation, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if he asks without knowing,
or if he does not speak because he is ill.
He does not say, "There will be strife, quarreling, contention, or dispute in the Saṅgha";
he does not say, "There will be a schism in the Saṅgha or a fracture in the Saṅgha";
he does not say, "They will perform an illegal act, or an act by an incomplete assembly, or an act against one who is ineligible for such an act."
[This applies] to one who is insane,
and to the first offender.
The second training rule concerning speaking otherwise is finished.
